Chapter 7: Parks, Playgrounds, and the Myth of Open Space.
Have you ever heard someone say that more parks and open spaces automatically make a city better? It sounds great, right? You picture green lawns, shady trees, and playgrounds where kids laugh and run wild. But, as it turns out, the real story is a bit more complicated.
Not all parks are created equal, and just having open space doesn’t always breathe life into a neighborhood. Think about a park you’ve seen that’s usually empty. The grass is perfect, the benches spotless, but hardly anyone sticks around. Parents might even hurry their kids past, feeling uneasy about the quiet. It’s almost as if the park is cut off from the rest of the city—a space that’s more of a barrier than a gathering place.
And then, there are those tiny playgrounds tucked between apartment buildings. They might not look fancy, but they’re alive with energy. You’ll see parents chatting while their kids dream up games with whatever’s lying around. People stop by on their way to work, or just to catch a break in the afternoon heat. What makes these playgrounds feel safe and welcoming? It’s simple—they’re visible, surrounded by homes and shops, with plenty of eyes keeping watch.
What really matters isn’t the size or style of a park, but how it connects to the neighborhood. Parks that sit isolated from daily life often end up neglected, or worse, they feel unsafe. But when a park or playground is woven into the street—where people naturally pass by and pause—it becomes a true hub for the community.
It’s easy to fall into the trap of thinking that open space is always a good thing. But too much empty space can actually drain the life out of a neighborhood, making it feel less safe and less connected. The best parks? They invite people in, feeling more like an extension of the sidewalk than a spot to escape from the city.
So, here’s the key takeaway: parks and playgrounds work best when they’re part of everyday routines and rhythms. They should be places people genuinely want to spend time—not just pretty dots on a map. When these spaces are designed with care, and with a real understanding of how folks live, they can truly become the heart of a neighborhood.
